## Proof

**Answer: Yes.** There exists a matrix $B$ commuting with $P$ satisfying $\|B - A\| \le 2\|[A,P]\|$.

### Construction

Define the "block-diagonal part" of $A$ with respect to $P$:

$$B \;=\; PAP + (I-P)A(I-P).$$

### Step 1: $B$ commutes with $P$

Using $P^2 = P$ and $(I-P)P = 0$:

$$BP = PAPP + (I-P)A\underbrace{(I-P)P}_{=0} = PAP,$$
$$PB = \underbrace{PP}_{=P}AP + \underbrace{P(I-P)}_{=0}A(I-P) = PAP.$$

Hence $BP = PB$, i.e., $[B,P] = 0$. ✓

### Step 2: Bounding $\|A - B\|$

Expand:

$$(I-P)A(I-P) = A - AP - PA + PAP,$$

so

$$B = PAP + A - AP - PA + PAP = A - AP - PA + 2PAP,$$

and therefore

$$A - B = AP + PA - 2PAP = \underbrace{(AP - PAP)}_{(I-P)AP} + \underbrace{(PA - PAP)}_{PA(I-P)}.$$

### Step 3: Relating the two terms to the commutator $[A,P] = AP - PA$

**First term.** Since $(I-P)P = 0$ and $P^2 = P$:

$$(I-P)[A,P]\,P = (I-P)(AP - PA)P = (I-P)AP - \underbrace{(I-P)PA}_{=\,0}P = (I-P)AP.$$

**Second term.** Since $P(I-P) = 0$:

$$P[A,P](I-P) = P(AP - PA)(I-P) = \underbrace{PAP(I-P)}_{=\,0} - PA(I-P) = -PA(I-P).$$

Combining:

$$A - B = (I-P)[A,P]\,P \;-\; P[A,P](I-P).$$

### Step 4: Norm estimate

Since $P$ and $I-P$ are self-adjoint projections, $\|P\| \le 1$ and $\|I-P\| \le 1$. By the triangle inequality and submultiplicativity:

$$\|A - B\| \;\le\; \|(I-P)\|\,\|[A,P]\|\,\|P\| \;+\; \|P\|\,\|[A,P]\|\,\|(I-P)\| \;\le\; 2\,\|[A,P]\|.$$

### Conclusion

For every $\varepsilon > 0$, if $\|[A,P]\| < \varepsilon/2$, the matrix $B = PAP + (I-P)A(I-P)$ satisfies $[B,P] = 0$ and $\|B - A\| \le 2\|[A,P]\| < \varepsilon$. Thus a matrix commuting with $P$ and arbitrarily close to $A$ always exists, with the explicit bound

$$\boxed{\|B - A\| \le 2\,\|[A,P]\|.}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
